source.title: Use of Sedative-Hypnotic Drugs and the Risk of Developing Alzheimer's Disease: A Systematic Review, Meta-Analysis and Meta-Regression
authors: M D V S do Nascimento

confidence_rationale: Recent, large, well-conducted systematic review with meta-regression -- the best available class-level test of IMPL-026's central risk ordering. Downgraded from higher because the headline association is design-dependent (OR 1.29, 95% CI 1.10-1.53 significant; HR-restricted 1.17, 95% CI 0.87-1.58 null), heterogeneity is severe (I2 86.5%), and the subgroup pattern actively contradicts one of IMPL-026's rows rather than merely under-determining it.
failure_signatures: Restricting to hazard ratios attenuates the sedative-hypnotic/AD association to non-significance (HR 1.17, 95% CI 0.87-1.58), so IMPL-026's blanket WORSENS assignments are not robust to study design.

Short-acting agents showed elevated AD risk while broad-acting benzodiazepines did not -- the opposite of IMPL-026's row ordering, which places classical benzodiazepines in the highest-risk tier on the strength of their SWS+REM suppression.
Between-study heterogeneity of I2 = 86.5% means the pooled point estimate should not be read as a stable class effect for any single row of the table.

The authors explicitly cannot separate a genuine drug effect from confounding by indication (prodromal insomnia as an early AD symptom), which is the reverse-causation pathway IMPL-026's mechanistic framing assumes away.

mapping.source_claim_statement: Pooled observational evidence associates sedative-hypnotic use with higher odds of Alzheimer's disease (OR 1.29; 95% CI 1.10-1.53; I2 = 86.5%), but the association is attenuated and non-significant when restricted to hazard-ratio estimates (HR 1.17; 95% CI 0.87-1.58; I2 = 73.1%); short-acting agents showed elevated risk whereas broad-acting benzodiazepines did not.
mapping.ree_translation: Read against IMPL-026, this is the closest thing to a direct test of the table's top-level claim that GABAergic/sedative agents carry a net WORSENS dementia-risk direction. It supports the sign of the effect at class level while refusing to support the table's confident row-by-row gradation -- and its short-acting/broad-acting split is orthogonal to the phase-disruption axis (MECH-173/MECH-174) that IMPL-026 uses to order the rows.
mapping.mapping_caveat: IMPL-026 classifies medications by PREDICTED phase-specific pipeline disruption (INV-045 Phase 0-4). This paper measures neither phase-resolved consolidation nor any REE pipeline quantity; the mapping runs from a clinical endpoint back to a mechanism the study did not observe. In particular, pharmacokinetic half-life -- the axis on which this meta-analysis found its subgroup signal -- is NOT the axis IMPL-026 classifies on, so a concordant overall sign masks a discordant internal structure.
mapping.source_context: Human pharmacoepidemiology; databases searched from inception to 16 August 2025; incident Alzheimer's disease endpoint.

confidence_components.notes: source_quality high for design and recency but capped by I2 = 86.5%. mapping_fidelity is the binding constraint: an incident-AD endpoint is several inferential steps from phase-specific pipeline disruption. transfer_risk moderate -- confounding by indication runs in the same direction as the hypothesised effect.
